title: SE 2025 Urban Form D Variables (H3)
text:
What it does
The “D variables” are a standard framework for measuring how urban form relates to travel behavior (Cervero and Kockelman, 1997; Ewing and Cervero, 2010). This project calculates them for the WFRC and MAG region from WFRC’s SE 2025 socioeconomic data, at H3 resolution 9 and 8.







Variable
What it measures




Density
Residents and workers per square mile


Diversity
Balance of homes and jobs (land-use mix)


Design
Street-network connectivity


Destinations
Proximity to activity centers and everyday amenities, with seven sub-components


Demographics
Median household income and an Income Diversity Index


Distance to transit
Distance to the nearest frequent-service stop



A supplementary Rental Housing Attainability Index, developed by Cascadia Partners with WFRC and UTA, is included alongside them.
Because urban form describes the environment a person experiences, not the contents of an arbitrary polygon, each variable is spatially smoothed across neighboring hexagons. The explorer’s swipe control compares the smoothed value with the raw one.

title: Housing Site Evaluator
text:
What it does
The Housing Site Evaluator helps housing and land-use planners see which places have good access to opportunity. Users choose their community, optionally filter by land use, and set priorities for eleven accessibility factors; the tool turns that into a heat map from most to least accessible.







Group
Factors




Employment
Auto access to jobs, transit access to jobs


Transportation
Transit stops, freeway exits, active transportation


Necessities
Childcare, healthcare, education, grocery stores, community centers, parks



Each factor is scored 0 to 1 per parcel and hexagon. Wasatch Choice center and Opportunity Zone layers are shown as context only; they are not part of the score.

Good morning! I’m Pukar Bhandari, and I’m excited to discuss how economic impact analysis can enhance WFRC’s already strong transportation planning capabilities.
I completed my graduate education here at the University of Utah in Transportation Planning, and over the past three years, I’ve specialized in developing methods that bridge transportation modeling with economic quantification. What really excites me about WFRC is the opportunity to support investment prioritization in one of the nation’s fastest-growing regions, contribute to 2034 Olympic legacy planning, and be part of your transition to activity-based modeling. My technical background in travel demand modeling with Cube and TransCAD, combined with economic impact tools like IMPLAN, positions me to contribute from day one.

Where I see an opportunity to add value is moving from asking “How does the system perform?” to “What does this investment do for our region’s economy?”
Traditional analysis focuses on travel time savings, VMT reduction, crash reduction, and emissions benefits. Enhanced analysis that I can bring adds regional job creation, economic multiplier effects, business attraction potential, and return on investment metrics.
This enhanced perspective doesn’t replace what you’re already doing well - it helps justify investments to stakeholders and supports competitive grant applications, which is increasingly important in today’s funding environment.

Economic Impact Framework I’ve Applied

    A["<b>Transportation Investment</b>"] --> B("Direct Construction<br>Stimulus") & C("User Cost Savings<br>Time • Crashes • Fuel") & D("Market Access Improvements<br>Larger Labor/Supplier Pool") & E("Business Attraction<br>Enhanced Site Competitiveness")

Key insight from my experience: Not all transportation benefits create wider economic impacts. Understanding this distinction helps prioritize projects that maximize both mobility and economic returns.



Here’s the systematic framework I’ve developed through my work. Transportation investments create economic impacts through four main pathways:
First, direct construction stimulus - the immediate jobs and spending from building infrastructure. Second, user cost savings - when people save time, reduce crashes, and spend less on fuel, that money gets reinvested in the economy. Third, market access improvements - better transportation expands labor pools and supplier networks for businesses. And fourth, business attraction - enhanced infrastructure makes locations more competitive for new investment.
All of these feed into broader regional economic impacts: jobs created, household income growth, business output increases, and GDP growth.
The key insight from my experience is that not all transportation benefits create wider economic impacts. Understanding this distinction helps prioritize projects that maximize both mobility and economic returns.

title: Quantifying Economic Effects of Transportation Investments
text:
Utah’s Unified Plan 2023-2050


What I contributed to Utah’s $88 billion transportation plan:






Key Results:

Construction phase: 70,000+ direct jobs
Societal Benefits: $230+ B present value (28 years)
Economic Impact: $490 B regional output increase (28 years)
Return Ratio: $5.57 economic activity per dollar invested annually



Relevance to WFRC: This same methodology can support WFRC’s RTP development, enhance travel demand modeling, and federal grant applications.

















Let me show you how this works in practice with Utah’s $88+ billion transportation plan.
My methodology integrated travel demand model outputs with benefit-cost analysis frameworks and economic impact analysis. I built custom R and Excel-based workflows that link transportation performance metrics directly to benefit-cost frameworks, integrate IMPLAN economic multipliers, and produce economic metrics, allowing for scenario-based analysis across multimodal investment alternatives.
The results were significant: construction phase impacts of over 70,000 direct jobs, operations phase benefits with $230 billion present value over 28 years, total economic impact of $490 billion in cumulative regional output increase, and a return ratio of $5.6 in economic activity per dollar invested.
This workflow produces clear, reproducible, data-driven impact reports that can directly support WFRC’s future RTP development, Olympic planning, and federal grant applications.

title: Analyzing the Utah Bikeways data
text:
This analysis examines the distribution of roadway and bikeway infrastructure across Utah municipalities. The primary objectives are to:

Calculate total road lane miles for each municipality
Calculate bikeway lane miles by facility type for each municipality
Compare roadway and bikeway infrastructure across municipalities

All spatial data is sourced from the Utah Geospatial Resource Center (UGRC) and processed using the R spatial ecosystem.

2.3 Environment Variables
We use EPSG:3566 (NAD83(HARN) / Utah North) projection, which uses US survey feet as the base unit. This projection is appropriate for statewide analysis in Utah and ensures accurate distance calculations.

# Set Project CRS
PROJECT_CRS = "EPSG:3566"

# Set tmap mode to interactive
tmap::tmap_mode("view")

title: Analyzing the Utah Bikeways data
text:
3.1 Utah City Boundaries
Municipal boundaries are used to aggregate roadway and bikeway data by city. These boundaries represent the legal limits of incorporated municipalities in Utah.

# Define paths
path_ut_cities <- file.path(dir_data, "UtahMunicipalBoundaries.gpkg")

# Download if not exists
if (!fs::file_exists(path_ut_cities)) {
  # Read data using arcgis package
  sf_ut_cities <- arc_read_retry(
    "https://services1.arcgis.com/99lidPhWCzftIe9K/ArcGIS/rest/services/UtahMunicipalBoundaries/FeatureServer/0",
    crs = PROJECT_CRS
  ) |> janitor::clean_names()
  # Write to a GeoDatabase
  sf_ut_cities |>
    sf::st_write(path_ut_cities, layer = "UtahMunicipalBoundaries", append = FALSE)
}

# Always read from the local copy, so the geometry column is the same
# whether the file was just downloaded or already existed
sf_ut_cities <- sf::st_read(path_ut_cities, quiet = TRUE) |>
  sf::st_transform(PROJECT_CRS)


tmap::qtm(sf_ut_cities)

Sprites are the other half. Highway shields and base icons are raster PNGs, which can’t be recolored through paint properties, so the generator reworks the sprite sheets too (inverting them for a dark theme, for example).

Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
Most of my day-to-day GIS work happens in R or Python: load a shapefile, write a few spatial queries, make a quick map to sanity-check the result. That is fast when you are already in a scripting environment, and annoying when you just want to look at a file, or hand someone a tool without asking them to install anything.
I wanted something simpler: open a file, write a SQL query, see the answer on a map. No server, no accounts, no desktop GIS. That itch became Spatial Explorer. It started in February as a single-page app inspired by Kyle Walker’s Spatial SQL Explorer, and it has since been rebuilt into a web app and a VS Code extension that share one engine. This post is about what it does now and why it is built the way it is.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
1 Try it
Use Try sample data for US counties, or drop in your own file. Everything runs in your tab.

  
    Spatial Explorer

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
2 What it does
The scope is deliberately small: look at a file, query it, style the result, export it.

LookQueryStyleAnalyzeExport and print



Formats: GeoJSON, GeoPackage (several layers), SQLite/SpatiaLite (Cube 7 networks, for example), FlatGeobuf, Shapefile, GeoParquet, Parquet, GML, CSV, PMTiles and Excel. File Geodatabases (experimental) and GTFS transit feeds open too, and a zip opens like the file inside it.
A map and an attribute table kept in sync, any source CRS, and 129 basemaps from 26 providers with real previews, plus a globe view.
One search box for layer values, coordinates and places.
Map tools: measure distances and areas, draw shapes to select or filter rows (or to use as a SQL table called drawn), and turn on terrain with hillshade and elevation. These are scratch geometry only; your data is never edited.



DuckDB spatial SQL runs against the file by its own name, with autocomplete and inline errors. Results replace the map and the table.
1SELECT * FROM us_counties
2SELECT * FROM layer
3SELECT * FROM us_boundaries.counties
4SELECT * FROM ST_Read('data/links.shp')

1

The open file us-counties.parquet is available under its cleaned-up name.

2

…and always as layer, whatever it is called.

3

A multi-layer file such as a GeoPackage exposes its layers as views in a schema named after the file.

4

Other files can be read in the same query: by workspace-relative path in VS Code, or files you have added in the web app.


There are also 24 ready-made snippets that fill in the open layer’s own table and column names, and a word search (ranked, with stemming) beside the plain text search.


Single, categorized, graduated (by a column or a SQL expression), continuous, as-is, bivariate, rule-based, heatmap and cluster styles, with ramps previewed on the map. Under Vary by attribute, several properties can each follow their own column (size, width, outline, shape, pattern, opacity, rotation), so one map can show roads colored by level of service and widened by traffic. Labels, layer opacity and 3D polygon extrusion are there too, and styles are saved as a QGIS .qml sidecar.



Grid cells: bin any layer into H3 hexagons or A5 equal-area pentagons, counted or averaged per cell, with a live preview and the SQL it writes.
Dot density: one dot stands for an amount you choose, placed at random inside its polygons, with up to six columns in their own colors.
A time slider that filters the map and table by a date column and plays across time, and arrows that show the direction of lines.



Export all, filtered or selected rows to GeoParquet, GeoPackage, GeoJSON, newline-delimited GeoJSON, FlatGeobuf, Shapefile, KML, CSV, Parquet, Excel or JSON, in any EPSG CRS. Print lays the map out as a page (paper size, title, legend, scale bar, north arrow, a table and chart of the rows, even an atlas with a page per feature) and saves PNG, PDF or SVG with editable text.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
3 One codebase, two shells
The first version was a single page of JavaScript with module-level state, and it showed. It worked, but sharing a link or restoring a session meant threading state through everything. When I wanted a VS Code extension, I rebuilt it so the engine and the interface don’t know which shell they are in.





flowchart TD
  W["apps/web<br>browser shell"] --> UI
  X["apps/vscode-ext<br>custom editor + webview"] --> UI
  UI["packages/ui<br>map, table, panels"] --> CORE
  CORE["packages/core<br>sources, queries, styles, export"] --> DB["DuckDB-WASM"]






packages/core and packages/ui are forbidden (by a lint rule) from importing vscode, touching the File API or using IndexedDB. Anything platform-specific goes through one interface, the HostAdapter: pick the theme, open files, read a file as bytes or a URL for range reads, save a file, persist state, set a status. The web app implements it with the browser; the extension implements it with the VS Code API. Each custom-editor webview gets its own DuckDB instance.
The stack is Svelte 5, Vite and strict TypeScript, MapLibre GL JS for the map, CodeMirror 6 for the SQL editor, Terra Draw for drawing, and DuckDB-WASM underneath.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
4 Running DuckDB in a webview
DuckDB-WASM is the heart of it: a WebAssembly build of the DuckDB analytical engine, including the spatial extension that provides ST_Within, ST_Intersects, ST_Transform and friends.
In the first version I leaned on multi-threading, which needs SharedArrayBuffer, which needs special response headers that GitHub Pages cannot set. A service worker (coi-serviceworker) papered over that. VS Code webviews can’t use that trick, so the rebuild uses the single-threaded DuckDB-WASM bundle in both shells. One engine configuration to test is worth more than the speed-up.
A few decisions followed from taking the engine seriously:

The engine is not bundled. DuckDB-WASM, its extensions (spatial, parquet, json, and the optional full-text search, H3 and A5) and sql.js are downloaded once from pinned URLs and checked against SHA-256 hashes recorded in the repo, then cached locally (Cache Storage on the web, extension storage in VS Code), so later starts work offline.
There is a known ceiling. The engine’s memory limit is about 3.1 GiB in both shells, which I measured rather than assumed, and the design works around it.
Reads are ranged where possible, so the whole file is not copied into the webview.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
section: 5 Big data without re-querying on every pan
text:
5 Big data without re-querying on every pan
Drawing a million features as GeoJSON would freeze any tab, and re-running a query on every pan is slow. The rule is a size threshold:

Results under 100,000 rows (and files under 100 MiB) are converted to GeoJSON once and drawn from memory.
Larger ones are drawn from vector tiles that DuckDB builds per tile with ST_AsMVT, served to MapLibre through a custom protocol handler. A “Load all” link is there if you really want everything.

That is how files with millions of rows and several gigabytes stay pannable.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
6 The query is the product
Several features that look like dialogs are really generators of SQL, and show you the SQL.
Grid cells bin a layer into H3 or A5 cells with a live preview. The SQL it writes is the same SQL a power user would write, so you can copy it, change it, and run it as a normal query. The result gets the same styling and export as any other.
Dot density is the best example. DuckDB has no point-in-polygon generator (ST_GeneratePoints takes a bounding box), so the query samples each polygon’s box with a deterministic hash(feature, column, k) and keeps the first n points that are ST_Within the polygon. Because the hash is deterministic, the map looks the same every time instead of reshuffling the dots on each redraw.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
7 Formats that fight back
File Geodatabases are the format I most wanted and the hardest to read. DuckDB-WASM’s GDAL build has the OpenFileGDB driver turned off for WebAssembly, so the SQL engine cannot open a .gdb at all, and it cannot read inside a zip either. The workaround is gdal3.js (GDAL 3.8.4 compiled to WebAssembly), downloaded only the first time you open a geodatabase, which converts the chosen layer so DuckDB can query it. In a spike on an 818 MB geodatabase it listed layers in 87 ms and converted 4 million parcels to FlatGeobuf in 34 seconds. Compressed (CDF/SDC) geodatabases remain unreadable by any open-source reader, so that format stays marked experimental.
GTFS feeds are detected by what is inside the zip (stops, routes, trips, stop times and their columns), never by file name, so GTFS.zip, google_transit.zip and data.zip all work. A feed opens as two layers drawn together, routes (lines, in each route’s own color) and stops (points), each its own table.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
8 Styles that travel
Styles are saved as a QGIS .qml sidecar, so a styled file looks right in QGIS too, and the app imports and exports QML, SLD and Mapbox GL style JSON. Labels are drawn with system fonts (nothing is downloaded), saved with the style, and included when you export the map image.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
9 What I’d say about scope
The project has an explicit list of things it will not do: feature editing, georeferencing, a processing toolbox, notebooks, plugins, raster analysis, stacked basemaps, multiple map layers. One layer is on the map at a time; multi-file work is done in SQL. Every exception (a globe projection, polygon extrusion, terrain) was a recorded decision. For a tool whose point is “never open QGIS for basic work”, staying a quick-look tool matters more than any one feature.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
10 Privacy and network use
Your data stays on your machine. The network is used for the engine’s code (downloaded once, then cached), for basemap tiles, and for an opt-out place search that sends only the text you type.

title: Spatial Explorer: Spatial SQL for Maps, in the Browser and in VS Code
text:
11 Wrapping up
The code is MIT-licensed on GitHub, and the changelog has the details of every release. The project owes a lot to GeoLibre and Qiusheng Wu, a constant reference for the style panel, basemap picker and data-loading design, and to Kyle Walker’s original Spatial SQL Explorer for the idea. If you work with spatial data and want a scratchpad that doesn’t need a server, give it a try. Issues and PRs welcome.

title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
text:
Population demographics are fundamental to transportation planning and urban analysis. Understanding age distributions helps inform infrastructure decisions, transit planning, and resource allocation. In this post, this blog will walk through building an interactive Shiny application that combines population pyramids with spatial visualization using {mapgl} package.
The app allows users to explore county-level demographic data across all US states, displaying both the geographic context through an interactive map and detailed age-sex distributions through population pyramids.

text:
Population demographics are fundamental to transportation planning and urban analysis. Understanding age distributions helps inform infrastructure decisions, transit planning, and resource allocation. In this post, this blog will walk through building an interactive Shiny application that combines population pyramids with spatial visualization using {mapgl} package.
The app allows users to explore county-level demographic data across all US states, displaying both the geographic context through an interactive map and detailed age-sex distributions through population pyramids.

title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
text:
2 Application Overview
The Population Pyramid Explorer features:

Interactive state selection with smooth map transitions
County-level demographic visualization using Census tract data for context
Dynamic population pyramids showing age-sex distributions
Responsive design using MapLibre’s story map format
Real-time data integration from the US Census Bureau

title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
text:
3 Repository and Code Access
The complete source code for this application is available on GitHub: Population Pyramid Explorer Repository
The repository includes additional documentation, deployment instructions, and example usage scenarios.

title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
text:
4 Key Dependencies and Setup
The application leverages several powerful R packages for data processing, spatial analysis, and visualization:
# Custom function to load packages, installing them first if not already installed
load_pkg <- function(pkg) {
  if (!require(pkg, character.only = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg)
  }
  library(pkg, character.only = TRUE)
}

# Data manipulation and visualization
load_pkg("dplyr")
load_pkg("tidyr") 
load_pkg("ggplot2")
load_pkg("scales")

# Spatial data and mapping
load_pkg("sf")
load_pkg("mapgl")
load_pkg("tigris")

# Census data integration
load_pkg("tidycensus")

# UI framework
load_pkg("shiny")
The load_pkg() function ensures packages are installed and loaded, making deployment more robust across different environments.

title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
text:
5 Application Architecture

User Interface Design
The UI implements {mapgl}’s story map concept, creating a scrollable narrative experience:
mapgl::story_maplibre(
  map_id = "map",
  font_family = "Poppins",
  sections = list(
    "intro" = mapgl::story_section(...),
    "state_detail" = mapgl::story_section(...)
  )
)
This approach provides intuitive navigation between the overview (state selection) and detailed analysis (county demographics).


Reactive Data Architecture
The server logic employs several reactive components that efficiently manage data flow:
State Geometry: Loads and transforms state boundaries using the Web Mercator projection (EPSG:3857) for optimal web mapping performance.
Census Tract Data: Dynamically fetches median age data at the tract level, providing geographic context for county selection. The data pipeline includes coordinate reference system transformation and popup content preparation.
Population Estimates: Retrieves detailed age-sex breakdowns from the Census Bureau’s Population Estimates API, specifically formatted for pyramid visualization.

title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
text:
6 Data Processing Pipeline

Geographic Data Preparation
The application processes spatial data through several key transformations:
states_sf <- tigris::states(cb = TRUE) |>
  sf::st_transform(crs = 3857) |>
  sf::st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM")
Using cartographic boundary files (cb = TRUE) provides simplified geometries that render faster while maintaining visual accuracy at the national scale.


Census Data Integration
The demographic data pipeline combines two Census Bureau APIs:

American Community Survey (ACS) for tract-level median age visualization
Population Estimates Program for detailed county-level age-sex distributions

The tract-level data provides spatial context with median age choropleth mapping, while county estimates power the detailed population pyramids.


Data Transformation for Visualization
Population pyramid data requires specific transformations:
dplyr::mutate(
  value = ifelse(SEX == "Male", -value, value),
  age_min = ifelse(
    stringr::str_detect(AGEGROUP, "under"), 0,
    as.numeric(stringr::str_extract(AGEGROUP, "\\d+"))
  )
)
Male populations receive negative values for the traditional pyramid layout, and age groups are parsed to enable proper ordering.

title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
text:
7 Interactive Mapping Features

Map Initialization and Styling
The base map uses Carto’s Voyager style for clean, readable cartography:
mapgl::maplibre(
  mapgl::carto_style("voyager"),
  center = c(-98.5, 39.5),
  zoom = 3,
  scrollZoom = FALSE
) |>
mapgl::set_projection(projection = "globe")
The globe projection adds visual appeal while the disabled scroll zoom prevents navigation conflicts with the story map interface.


Dynamic Layer Management
Map layers update responsively based on user selections:

State boundaries provide national context with selective highlighting
Census tract fills show median age patterns using a continuous color scale
Interactive popups display detailed demographic information

The color scheme uses ColorBrewer’s spectral palette, providing intuitive age visualization from young (red) to old (purple).


Smooth Transitions
Section-based navigation triggers smooth map animations:
mapgl::fly_to(
  center = c(-98.5, 39.5),
  zoom = 3,
  bearing = 0,
  pitch = 0,
  duration = 1500
)
These transitions maintain user orientation while providing engaging visual feedback.

title: Building an Interactive Population Pyramid Explorer
text:
8 Population Pyramid Visualization

Chart Design Philosophy

Overture Maps Foundation provides a collaborative, open-source initiative to create the world’s most comprehensive and interoperable geospatial dataset. This post demonstrates how to efficiently download Overture Maps data using both R and Python with DuckDB’s powerful spatial capabilities.

Overture Maps is an open-source mapping initiative that provides global-scale geospatial data across four main themes:


Buildings: Footprints and building parts

Transportation: Road segments and connectors

Places: Points of interest and place data

Admins: Administrative boundaries and localities

overture_data <- function(bbox, overture_type, dst_parquet) {

  # Validate overture_type
  if (!overture_type %in% names(map_themes)) {

  }

  # Configure S3 path
  s3_region <- "us-west-2"
  base_url <- sprintf("s3://overturemaps-%s/release", s3_region)
  version <- "2024-04-16-beta.0"
  theme <- map_themes[[overture_type]]
  remote_path <- sprintf("%s/%s/theme=%s/type=%s/*", base_url, version, theme, overture_type)

  # Connect to DuckDB and install extensions
  conn <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
  DBI::dbExecute(conn, "INSTALL httpfs;")
  DBI::dbExecute(conn, "INSTALL spatial;")
  DBI::dbExecute(conn, "LOAD httpfs;")
  DBI::dbExecute(conn, "LOAD spatial;")
  DBI::dbExecute(conn, sprintf("SET s3_region='%s';", s3_region))

  # Create view and execute spatial query
  read_parquet <- sprintf("read_parquet('%s', filename=TRUE, hive_partitioning=1);", remote_path)
  DBI::dbExecute(conn, sprintf("CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW data_view AS SELECT * FROM %s", read_parquet))

  query <- sprintf("

    FROM data_view AS data
    WHERE data.bbox.xmin <= %f AND data.bbox.xmax >= %f
    AND data.bbox.ymin <= %f AND data.bbox.ymax >= %f
  ", bbox[3], bbox[1], bbox[4], bbox[2])

  # Save results to Parquet file
  file <- normalizePath(dst_parquet, mustWork = FALSE)
  DBI::dbExecute(conn, sprintf("COPY (%s) TO '%s' WITH (FORMAT 'parquet');", query, file))
  DBI::dbDisconnect(conn, shutdown = TRUE)
}




def overture_data(bbox, overture_type, dst_parquet):
    """Query a subset of Overture's data and save it as a GeoParquet file.

    Parameters
    ----------
    bbox : tuple
        A tuple of floats representing the bounding box (xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)
        in EPSG:4326 coordinate reference system.
    overture_type : str
        The type of Overture data to query
    dst_parquet : str or Path
        The path to the output GeoParquet file.
    """
    if overture_type not in map_themes:
        raise ValueError(f"Valid Overture types are: {list(map_themes)}")

    # Configure S3 connection
    s3_region = "us-west-2"
    base_url = f"s3://overturemaps-{s3_region}/release"
    version = "2024-04-16-beta.0"
    theme = map_themes[overture_type]
    remote_path = f"{base_url}/{version}/theme={theme}/type={overture_type}/*"

    # Setup DuckDB with spatial extensions
    conn = duckdb.connect()
    conn.execute("INSTALL httpfs;")
    conn.execute("INSTALL spatial;")
    conn.execute("LOAD httpfs;")
    conn.execute("LOAD spatial;")
    conn.execute(f"SET s3_region='{s3_region}';")

    # Execute spatial query
    read_parquet = f"read_parquet('{remote_path}', filename=true, hive_partitioning=1);"
    conn.execute(f"CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW data_view AS SELECT * FROM {read_parquet}")

    query = f"""
    SELECT data.*
    FROM data_view AS data
    WHERE data.bbox.xmin <= {bbox[2]} AND data.bbox.xmax >= {bbox[0]}
    AND data.bbox.ymin <= {bbox[3]} AND data.bbox.ymax >= {bbox[1]}
    """

    file = str(Path(dst_parquet).resolve())
    conn.execute(f"COPY ({query}) TO '{file}' WITH (FORMAT PARQUET);")

Raster Conversion and Matrix Preparation
The conversion from vector hexagon data to raster format is essential for rayshader’s 3D rendering capabilities. This process involves calculating optimal dimensions while preserving the geographic aspect ratio.

# Calculate bounding box and aspect ratio
bbox <- sf::st_bbox(nepal_boundary)

# Define corner points for aspect ratio calculation
bottom_left <- sf::st_point(c(bbox[["xmin"]], bbox[["ymin"]])) |>
  sf::st_sfc(crs = project_crs)
bottom_right <- sf::st_point(c(bbox[["xmax"]], bbox[["ymin"]])) |>
  sf::st_sfc(crs = project_crs)
top_left <- sf::st_point(c(bbox[["xmin"]], bbox[["ymax"]])) |>
  sf::st_sfc(crs = project_crs)

# Calculate dimensions
width <- sf::st_distance(bottom_left, bottom_right)
height <- sf::st_distance(bottom_left, top_left)

# Determine aspect ratios
if(width > height) {
  w_ratio <- 1
  h_ratio <- height / width
} else {
  h_ratio <- 1
  w_ratio <- width / height
}

# Convert to raster with optimal resolution

                          nx = floor(size * w_ratio),
                          ny = floor(size * h_ratio))

# Create matrix for 3D rendering
pop_matrix <- matrix(pop_raster$population,
                    nrow = floor(size * w_ratio),
                    ncol = floor(size * h_ratio))

title: A Zero-Cost Freight Flow Explorer for Utah
text:
The Freight Analysis Framework (FAF) is the go-to public source for how much freight moves between U.S. regions, by commodity and mode. It is also awkward to use: several releases with different zone systems, benchmark years and dollar bases, plus a forecast that skips 2025 to 2029. Answering “what moves in and out of Utah?” usually means downloading gigabytes and wrangling them yourself.
So I built an explorer that does the wrangling once and ships the result as a static site. Utah is the configured state; adding another is a one-file change.

title: A Zero-Cost Freight Flow Explorer for Utah
text:
2 What it shows

Origin-destination flows in tons, value and ton-miles for every record that touches the state, by commodity, mode and year. FAF5.7.1 (2017 to 2050) and FAF6.0 (2022) are kept apart, never combined on one axis.
Forecast scenarios: the mid-range forecast plus FAF5’s published High and Low scenarios, with forecast and preliminary years marked and the unpublished 2025 to 2029 shown as a gap.
Linked charts instead of tables: direction, mode and commodity (treemap), the largest partner states, trends with the scenario band, a commodity-by-year heat map, and a two-year comparison. Clicking any element filters everything else.
The FAF5 truck network with modeled link volumes, and clearly labeled experimental county-level estimates for 2022.







ImportantData and caveats only



The app does not rank places, score performance, or present modeled values as measured counts. FAF flows are modeled estimates, and the app says so wherever they appear.

title: A Zero-Cost Freight Flow Explorer for Utah
text:
3 How it works
Nothing runs on a server. A local pipeline turns the raw federal files into Parquet, and the browser queries those files directly over HTTP range requests.





flowchart LR
  A["BTS / FHWA / ORNL / Census files"] --> B["pipeline/<br>Python + DuckDB"]
  B -->|"validate"| C["Deterministic Parquet,<br>GeoJSON, PMTiles"]
  C --> D["GitHub Pages<br>docs/"]
  D --> E["Browser<br>DuckDB-WASM + MapLibre"]






The pipeline is a small command-line tool run with uv:
cd pipeline
1uv run python -m faf_pipeline update --state utah
2uv run python -m faf_pipeline fetch --state utah --check-only
3uv run python -m faf_pipeline validate --state utah
4uv run pytest

1

Fetch, build, zones, county estimates, network and validation in one go. It prints a changelog of what changed.

2

Report changed files and new FAF releases without downloading anything.

3

Run the checks that must pass before processed data is committed.

4

Unit tests run on tiny fixture files for a fictional state.


Three design choices made the rest easy:

Deterministic output. Re-running update on unchanged inputs produces byte-identical files, so a second run leaves no git diff and every data change is reviewable.
A schema guard. Every downloaded file’s columns are checked against a column map, so a new release that renames or drops a column fails loudly instead of quietly corrupting results.
No state literals in the code. Utah appears only in config/states/utah.yml; validation fails if a state name, abbreviation or zone id shows up as a literal elsewhere.

title: Drut: Linting and Formatting for Cube Voyager Scripts
text:
WarningUnder active development



Drut is a work in progress. If you hit a bug, please open an issue.
Travel-demand models are programs. In much of the U.S., the language they are written in is Cube Voyager’s control-statement script (.s and .block files), and the tooling for it is thin: usually no syntax highlighting, no error checking until the model actually runs, and no consistent formatting across a team. A missing ENDIF can cost you a full model run to find.
Drut is my attempt to give those scripts the tooling that every mainstream language takes for granted.

title: Drut: Linting and Formatting for Cube Voyager Scripts
text:
1 What it does

Syntax highlighting from a static TextMate grammar, so it works even before the language server starts. Control words, function calls, keyword=value pairs, data references (MI, MW, DBA, ZONES) and user variables are each independently recolorable.
Structural diagnostics: unmatched IF/LOOP/RUN/PROCESS blocks, unclosed comments and similar real mistakes, flagged as you type, before you run the model.
Formatting: consistent indentation and, optionally, casing for control words, pair keywords, data references and function names, on save, on paste or from the CLI.
Hover, autocomplete and “did you mean” spell-check for control words and keyword names, plus code folding for every block kind.
Shared project configuration through a drut.toml, so a team does not have to agree on CLI flags or editor settings one by one.

A formatter that rewrites model code has to be easy to hold back, so a range can be excluded with markers. Everything between them is left exactly as written:
; FMT: OFF
  ... a hand-aligned section you want to keep as is ...
; FMT: ON

text:
In this workflow, we tackle a common geospatial problem: extracting data from stylized news graphics (like election heatmaps) and converting them into GIS-ready formats.
Rather than just cleaning the rough edges of a scraped SVG, we will use a reconstruction technique. We will:


Scrape the electoral map to get rough constituency shapes.

Georeferencing the shapes to align them with real coordinates.

text:
In this workflow, we tackle a common geospatial problem: extracting data from stylized news graphics (like election heatmaps) and converting them into GIS-ready formats.
Rather than just cleaning the rough edges of a scraped SVG, we will use a reconstruction technique. We will:

title: Nepal Electoral Constituency GeoJSON
text:
2 1. Setup and Libraries
We use sf for spatial operations and rvest for scraping. We also define paths for our inputs (official ward data) and outputs.

library(sf)       # Spatial data handling
library(xml2)     # Parsing XML/SVG
library(rvest)    # Web scraping

library(stringr)  # String manipulation
library(dplyr)    # Data manipulation

wards_geojson_path    <- here::here(post_dir, "data", "nepal-wards.gpkg")
national_geojson_path <- here::here(post_dir, "data", "nepal-national.gpkg")

# 3. Define output paths
output_svg_path       <- here::here(post_dir, "output", "nepal_electoral_map.svg")
rough_map_path <- here::here(post_dir, "output", "nepal_svg_rough.geojson")
output_geojson_path   <- here::here(post_dir, "output", "nepal_electoral_map.geojson")

# Ensure output directory exists
if (!dir.exists(dirname(output_svg_path))) dir.create(dirname(output_svg_path), recursive = TRUE)

title: Nepal Electoral Constituency GeoJSON
Nepal Electoral Constituency GeoJSON
Nepal Electoral Constituency GeoJSON
text:
5 Georeferencing (Affine Transformation)
The extracted SVG uses screen coordinates (pixels). To make this map useful, we must align it with the real world (Longitude/Latitude).
We do this by calculating the bounding box of a reference map (data/nepal-national.geojson) and scaling our SVG to fit those dimensions.

# 1. Load Reference Map
if (!file.exists(national_geojson_path)) stop("Reference map not found.")

nepal_ref <- st_read(national_geojson_path, quiet = TRUE)

# 2. Project Reference to Web Mercator (EPSG:3857)
# This gives us the correct target aspect ratio for a web map
target_bbox <- st_bbox(st_transform(nepal_ref, 3857))

# 3. Affine Transformation
# Flip Y-axis (SVG top-left origin -> Map bottom-left origin)
flip_matrix <- matrix(c(1, 0, 0, -1), ncol = 2)
nepal_sf$geometry <- nepal_sf$geometry * flip_matrix

# Calculate Scale Factors
src_bbox <- st_bbox(nepal_sf)
src_w <- src_bbox$xmax - src_bbox$xmin
src_h <- src_bbox$ymax - src_bbox$ymin

tgt_w <- target_bbox$xmax - target_bbox$xmin
tgt_h <- target_bbox$ymax - target_bbox$ymin

# Shift SVG to (0,0)
nepal_sf$geometry <- nepal_sf$geometry - c(src_bbox$xmin, src_bbox$ymin)

# Scale to match Reference size
scale_matrix <- matrix(c(tgt_w / src_w, 0, 0, tgt_h / src_h), ncol = 2)
nepal_sf$geometry <- nepal_sf$geometry * scale_matrix

# Shift to Reference position
nepal_sf$geometry <- nepal_sf$geometry + c(target_bbox$xmin, target_bbox$ymin)

# 4. Assign CRS (Web Mercator)
st_crs(nepal_sf) <- 3857


# Create interactive map
mapview::mapview(nepal_sf)






# Save the georeferenced SVG map before the ward dissolve
# We use 'delete_dsn = TRUE' to overwrite any old versions
st_write(
    nepal_sf,
    rough_map_path,
    driver = "GeoJSON",
    delete_dsn = TRUE,
    quiet = TRUE
)

message("Rough SVG map saved to: ", rough_map_path)

title: Nepal Electoral Constituency GeoJSON
text:
6 Reconstruction via Wards
The transformed SVG is roughly accurate but has “jagged” borders and low-quality topology. To fix this, we use the Wards method:

Convert high-quality Ward polygons to centroids.
Check which rough SVG shape each Ward centroid falls into.
Dissolve (merge) the Ward polygons based on that grouping.

This results in a map that perfectly matches official administrative boundaries.

message("Reconstructing boundaries using Wards...")

# 1. Load Wards Data
if (!file.exists(wards_geojson_path)) stop("Wards GeoJSON not found.")
wards <- st_read(wards_geojson_path, quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_make_valid()

# 2. Project to Metric (UTM Zone 45N) for accurate cleanup
# Nepal falls mostly in UTM 45N (EPSG:32645)
wards_utm <- st_transform(wards, 32645)
nepal_utm <- st_transform(nepal_sf, 32645) |> st_make_valid()

# 3. Assign Wards to Constituencies
message("Matching wards to constituencies...")
sf_use_s2(FALSE) # Use GEOS for the join
ward_centroids <- st_centroid(wards_utm)
nearest_indices <- st_nearest_feature(ward_centroids, nepal_utm)
wards_utm$constituency_id <- nepal_utm$constituency_id[nearest_indices]

# 4. Dissolve and Clean Slivers
message("Dissolving geometries and removing slivers...")

# SNAP TO GRID: Rounds coordinates to nearest 1mm to prevent tiny float errors
# wards_utm <- st_set_precision(wards_utm, 1000)

final_map_utm <- wards_utm |>
  group_by(constituency_id) |>
  summarise(geometry = st_union(geom)) |>
  st_make_valid() |>
  # SLIVER REMOVAL: 1 meter expansion and contraction
  st_buffer(dist = 1) |>
  st_buffer(dist = -1) |>
  st_make_valid()

# 5. Transform back to WGS84 for GeoJSON export
final_map <- st_transform(final_map_utm, 4326)


# Create interactive map. The widget embeds every vertex in the page, so map a
# simplified copy (200 m tolerance). The exported GeoJSON below stays full resolution.
final_map_preview <- final_map_utm |>
  sf::st_simplify(preserveTopology = TRUE, dTolerance = 200) |>
  st_transform(4326)

mapview::mapview(final_map_preview)






# 6. Save Result
st_write(
    final_map,
    output_geojson_path,
    driver = "GeoJSON",
    layer_options = "COORDINATE_PRECISION=6",
    delete_dsn = TRUE,
    quiet = TRUE
)

message("Reconstruction Complete! Saved to: ", output_geojson_path)

title: Building a Client-Side Open Matrix (OMX) File Viewer
text:
I spent way too long writing one-off Python scripts everytime I had to check what’s inside an OMX (Open Matrix Format) file. There had to be a better way.
So, I built a browser tool to preview OMX files directly. You can: - Browse individual matrices as separate tabs - Navigate to a specific row/col and see that cell’s value across all matrices at once - Run aggregations (sum, mean, median, etc.) across zones or across matrices - Do basic matrix arithmetic and export results

title: Building a Client-Side Geo/Parquet File Viewer
text:
Want a quick way to preview what is inside your parquet file? This is a browser-based, zero-backend viewer for Parquet and GeoParquet, built on DuckDB-WASM. Nothing is uploaded; everything runs locally in your tab.

3.4 2020 NCES school and college enrollment data
The National Center for Education Statistics provides comprehensive educational institution data including enrollment and staffing information for transportation planning analysis.
Public schools
Public school data is made available by National Center for Education Statistics through their Common Core of Data (CCD) program. For ease of processing, we retrieve the CCD from the ArcGIS REST service for the 2019-2020 academic year. The dataset includes total student enrollment and full-time equivalent teacher counts for each institution within the six-county region. Public schools represent major trip generation sources for both student and employee travel, requiring precise spatial location data for accurate modeling. > For more information on the NCES Public School data, refer to CCD Online Documentation.
To retrieve the data, we check if a local copy exists to ensure reproducibility and offline capability. If unavailable, we query the ArcGIS REST service and save a local copy.

Code# Create function to read ArcGIS FeatureLayer or Table
def arc_read(url, where="1=1", outFields="*", outSR=4326, **kwargs):
    """
    Read an ArcGIS FeatureLayer or Table to a GeoDataFrame.
    """

    # Ensure URL ends with /query
    if not url.endswith('/query'):
        url = url.rstrip('/') + '/query'

    # Build query parameters
    params = {
        'where': where,
        'outFields': outFields,
        'returnGeometry': 'true',
        # 'geometryType': 'esriGeometryPoint',
        'outSR': outSR,
        'f': 'geojson'
    }

    # Add any additional parameters
    params.update(kwargs)

    # Make request
    response = requests.get(url, params=params)

    # Read as GeoDataFrame
    return gpd.read_file(response.text)

4.1 Household-weighted interpolation
The interpolation process transfers ACS block group data to individual census blocks using household counts as weights. This method ensures that socioeconomic characteristics are distributed proportionally based on residential density rather than simple geometric overlay. Codedef interpolate_pw(from_gdf, to_gdf, weights_gdf, to_id=None, extensive=True,
                   weight_column=None, weight_placement='surface', crs=None):
    """
    Population-weighted areal interpolation between geometries.
    (Full function implementation hidden for brevity)
    """

    # Input validation
    if not all(isinstance(gdf, gpd.GeoDataFrame) for gdf in [from_gdf, to_gdf, weights_gdf]):
        raise ValueError("All inputs must be GeoDataFrames")

    # Make copies to avoid modifying originals
    from_gdf = from_gdf.copy()
    to_gdf = to_gdf.copy()
    weights_gdf = weights_gdf.copy()

    # Set CRS if provided
    if crs:
        from_gdf = from_gdf.to_crs(crs)
        to_gdf = to_gdf.to_crs(crs)
        weights_gdf = weights_gdf.to_crs(crs)

    # Check CRS consistency
    if not (from_gdf.crs == to_gdf.crs == weights_gdf.crs):
        raise ValueError("All inputs must have the same CRS")

    # Handle to_id
    if to_id is None:
        to_id = 'id'
        to_gdf[to_id] = to_gdf.index.astype(str)

    # Remove conflicting columns
    if to_id in from_gdf.columns:
        from_gdf = from_gdf.drop(columns=[to_id])

    # Create unique from_id
    from_id = 'from_id'
    from_gdf[from_id] = from_gdf.index.astype(str)

    # Handle weight column
    if weight_column is None:
        weight_column = 'interpolation_weight'
        weights_gdf[weight_column] = 1.0
    else:
        # Rename to avoid conflicts
        weights_gdf['interpolation_weight'] = weights_gdf[weight_column]
        weight_column = 'interpolation_weight'

    # Convert weights to points if needed
    if weights_gdf.geometry.geom_type.iloc[0] in ['Polygon', 'MultiPolygon']:
        if weight_placement == 'surface':
            weights_gdf = weights_gdf.copy()
            weights_gdf.geometry = weights_gdf.geometry.representative_point()
        elif weight_placement == 'centroid':
            weights_gdf = weights_gdf.copy()
            weights_gdf.geometry = weights_gdf.geometry.centroid
        else:
            raise ValueError("weight_placement must be 'surface' or 'centroid'")

    # Keep only weight column and geometry
    weight_points = weights_gdf[[weight_column, 'geometry']].copy()

    # Calculate denominators (total weights per source geometry)
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.filterwarnings('ignore', category=UserWarning)
        source_weights = gpd.sjoin(from_gdf, weight_points, how='left', predicate='contains')

    denominators = (source_weights.groupby(from_id)[weight_column]
                   .sum()
                   .reset_index()
                   .rename(columns={weight_column: 'weight_total'}))

    # Calculate intersections between from and to
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.filterwarnings('ignore', category=UserWarning)
        intersections = gpd.overlay(from_gdf, to_gdf, how='intersection')

    # Filter to keep only polygon intersections
    intersections = intersections[intersections.geometry.geom_type.isin(['Polygon', 'MultiPolygon', 'GeometryCollection'])]

    if len(intersections) == 0:
        raise ValueError("No valid polygon intersections found between source and target geometries")

    # Add intersection ID
    intersections['intersection_id'] = range(len(intersections))

    # Spatial join intersections with weight points to get weights within each intersection
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.filterwarnings('ignore', category=UserWarning)
        intersection_weights = gpd.sjoin(intersections, weight_points, how='left', predicate='contains')

    # Calculate intersection values (sum of weights per intersection)
    intersection_values = (intersection_weights.groupby('intersection_id')[weight_column]
                         .sum()
                         .reset_index()
                         .rename(columns={weight_column: 'intersection_value'}))

    # Merge back to intersections and keep only unique intersections
    intersections = intersections.merge(intersection_values, on='intersection_id', how='left')
    intersections['intersection_value'] = intersections['intersection_value'].fillna(0)

    # Remove duplicates created by the spatial join
    intersections = intersections.drop_duplicates(subset='intersection_id')

    # Merge with denominators to calculate weight coefficients
    intersections = intersections.merge(denominators, on=from_id, how='left')
    intersections['weight_total'] = intersections['weight_total'].fillna(1)

    # Calculate weight coefficients (intersection weight / total weight in source)
    intersections.loc[intersections['weight_total'] > 0, 'weight_coef'] = (
        intersections['intersection_value'] / intersections['weight_total']
    )
    intersections['weight_coef'] = intersections['weight_coef'].fillna(0)

    # Get numeric columns from source data
    numeric_cols = from_gdf.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns
    # Remove ID columns
    numeric_cols = [col for col in numeric_cols if col not in [from_id]]

    # Prepare intersection data for interpolation
    intersection_data = intersections[[from_id, to_id, 'weight_coef'] + numeric_cols].copy()

    if extensive:
        # For extensive variables: multiply by weight coefficient, then sum by target
        for col in numeric_cols:
            intersection_data[col] = intersection_data[col] * intersection_data['weight_coef']

        interpolated = (intersection_data.groupby(to_id)[numeric_cols]
                       .sum()
                       .reset_index())
    else:
        # For intensive variables: weighted average
        interpolated_data = []
        for target_id in intersection_data[to_id].unique():
            target_data = intersection_data[intersection_data[to_id] == target_id]
            if len(target_data) > 0 and target_data['weight_coef'].sum() > 0:
                weighted_vals = {}
                for col in numeric_cols:
                    weighted_vals[col] = (target_data[col] * target_data['weight_coef']).sum() / target_data['weight_coef'].sum()
                weighted_vals[to_id] = target_id
                interpolated_data.append(weighted_vals)

        interpolated = pd.DataFrame(interpolated_data)

    # Merge with target geometries
    result = to_gdf[[to_id, 'geometry']].merge(interpolated, on=to_id, how='left')

    # Fill NaN values with 0 for missing interpolations
    for col in numeric_cols:
        if col in result.columns:
            result[col] = result[col].fillna(0)

    return result

title: Evaluating Social Equity of Transit Accessibility: A Case of Salt Lake County, U.S.
text: Addressing social equity in public transportation remains a key challenge for many cities and planning organizations. In this study, we examined social equity dimensions of accessibility to light rail transit (LRT) stations in Salt Lake County, U.S., by employing two novel methods. First, we used the two-step floating catchment area (2SFCA) method to examine the interactions between the demand and supply of the public transit service. Second, we developed geospatial models to account for spatial bias in transit equity analysis. Results showed little evidence of inequitable access to LRT stations in Salt Lake County. The accessibility to LRT stations appeared to be generally higher in the downtown and transit catchment areas with a higher concentration of low-income and ethnic minority populations. Furthermore, we found statistically significant associations between higher transit accessibility and households which are not homeowners, and/or do not own a private motor vehicle. Our findings suggest that transit investments in Salt Lake County could leverage substantial transportation accessibility opportunities to achieve an equitable and sustainable future.

title: Prompt Engineering Best Practices
text:
Why This Talk?

“The difference between a good LLM output and a great one is almost never the model — it’s the prompt.”



Most of us are brute-forcing our chats
Copy → paste → pray → re-paste
Today: move to structured, repeatable prompt engineering
10 minutes to level up your LLM workflow


[~1 min]
Welcome everyone. Quick show of hands — how many of you used ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini at least once this week? Great. Now, how many of you feel like you’re getting the best possible output every time? Probably fewer hands.
That gap is what this talk is about. Most of us — myself included when I started — treat LLMs like a search engine. You type something in, get something back, and if it’s not right, you rephrase and try again. That’s brute-forcing.
Today I want to give you a set of concrete, practical techniques that will dramatically improve the quality of what you get back — especially for the kind of work we do: R scripts, Python pipelines, SQL queries, spatial analysis, travel demand modeling. All of these have specific patterns where prompt engineering makes a huge difference.
We’ll cover seven techniques in 10 minutes. Each one is immediately usable. Let’s go.

title: Prompt Engineering Best Practices
text:
1 · Context & Role Prompting


❌ Without Role
Write an R script to join 
traffic counts to TAZ polygons.
Generic, may use wrong packages, ignores projection issues

✅ With Role
Act as an expert transportation 
data scientist using R with sf.
I work with WFRC TAZ shapefiles 
(UTM 12N, EPSG:26912) and AADT 
count stations as point data.

Write an R script to spatially 
join traffic counts to TAZ polygons 
using the base pipe operator.


When you DON’T need it: quick syntax lookups, simple factual questions

[~1.5 min]
This is technique number one and it’s arguably the highest-leverage thing you can do. When you set a role, you are essentially telling the LLM which part of its training data to weight most heavily.
Look at the difference on screen. The left side — “write an R script to join traffic counts to TAZ polygons” — is going to give you something. But it might use merge() instead of sf::st_join(). It might not handle CRS transformations. It might use tidyverse pipes when you want base R pipes.
The right side gives the LLM three critical pieces of context: WHO you want it to be (an expert transportation data scientist), WHAT tools you’re using (R with sf, base pipe), and WHAT your data looks like (WFRC TAZ shapefiles in UTM 12N, point data for counts). Now the LLM knows to use st_join(), to check st_crs(), and to write idiomatic base-pipe R code.
When do you NOT need this? If you’re just asking “what’s the syntax for dplyr::case_when()?” — skip the role. Quick syntax lookups don’t benefit from a paragraph of preamble. Use your judgment: the more complex and domain-specific the task, the more a role prompt pays off.
One tip: save your best role prompts somewhere — a text file, a snippet manager, a pinned Slack message. You’ll reuse them constantly.

title: Prompt Engineering Best Practices
text:
2 · Plan First, Implement Second


Brute-Force
Write a Python script to process 
the household travel survey, 
calculate average trip lengths 
by mode and income group, and 
export the results for Cube.
One shot → bugs, missed edge cases

Chain of Thought
I need to process the WFRC 
household travel survey (CSV) 
and calculate average trip lengths 
by mode and income group for 
Cube Voyager import.

STEP 1: Outline the logical steps 
you would take. Do NOT write code 
yet. List assumptions.

STEP 2: Wait for my approval 
before writing the Python code.


Why it works: You catch logic errors before they’re buried in 200 lines of code.

[~1.5 min]
This is one of the most powerful techniques and it comes straight from the research literature — it’s called “Chain of Thought” or “Plan and Solve” prompting. The core idea is simple: force the LLM to think before it codes.
On the left, you’re asking the LLM to do everything in one shot. It has to figure out the data structure, decide how to handle missing values, choose aggregation logic, format the output for Cube — all simultaneously. That’s where bugs hide.
On the right, you explicitly break it into two phases. “First, outline the steps. List your assumptions. Wait for my approval.” This does three things:
First, it surfaces the LLM’s assumptions. Maybe it assumes trip length is in miles when your survey uses kilometers. Maybe it drops records with missing income instead of categorizing them as “Unknown.” You catch these before a single line of code is written.
Second, it creates a plan you can edit. “Actually, we also need to filter out trips under 0.1 miles — those are likely GPS noise.” Now the LLM incorporates that into its implementation.
Third, it often produces better code because the LLM has already organized its thinking. This is especially true for complex multi-step tasks like building a mode choice utility calculation or processing GTFS feeds.
This is a mindset shift: use the LLM as a collaborator, not a vending machine.

title: Prompt Engineering Best Practices
text:
3 · File Uploads & Data Privacy


✅ Safe to Upload

R scripts, Python notebooks, .qmd files
WFRC public GitHub repos
Published documentation & specs
SQL query logic (no credentials!)

⛔ Do NOT Upload

Raw survey respondent data
Personally identifiable information (PII)
Proprietary model parameters
Internal HR / financial records


The Workaround
# Share a SCHEMA, not the data:
"My data looks like this:

hh_id | persons | income_group
  int |     int | chr (Low/Med/High)
veh   | lat     | lng
  int |   dbl   | dbl

~45,000 rows. Some NAs in 
income_group (~8%). 
Write an R script to impute 
missing income using a 
k-nearest neighbors approach 
based on persons, veh, lat, lng."


[~1.5 min]
This slide is critical, and I want everyone to internalize this. Uploading files to LLMs is incredibly powerful — Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini can all read your code files directly. But there’s a bright line between code and data.
Code is almost always safe. Our WFRC repositories are public on GitHub. Your R scripts, your Python notebooks, your Quarto documents — upload them freely. The LLM can read the whole file, understand context, and give you much better help than if you paste a snippet.
Data is where you have to be careful. The household travel survey contains home locations, trip origins and destinations, income, household composition. That is sensitive data. Even if the LLM provider says they don’t train on your uploads, you are still transmitting that data over the internet to a third-party server. Don’t do it.
The workaround is on the right side of the screen: share a schema, not the data. Describe your columns, data types, approximate row count, and the nature of any quality issues like missing values. This gives the LLM everything it needs to write correct code without ever seeing a single real record.
Another option: create a small fake dataset. Use R to generate 50 synthetic rows with sample() and runif() that mimic the real structure. Upload that. The LLM writes code against it, and you run it on the real data locally.
One more note on context window bloat: if you upload a 10,000-line script, the LLM is spending most of its attention budget just holding that file in memory. Be selective. Upload the specific module or function you need help with, not the entire codebase.

title: Prompt Engineering Best Practices
text:
4 · Managing Long Contexts


The Problem
 Message 1: "Here's my R script..."
 Message 5: "Now add mode share..."
 Message 12: "Why did you forget 
              the CRS transform 
              from slide 1?"
 Message 18: 🤯 Complete nonsense
LLMs lose coherence as conversations grow.

The Fix: Summarize & Restart
Summarize our conversation so far:
- What script are we building?
- What variables and data are 
  involved?
- What's working and what's not?

Format it so I can paste it into 
a brand new chat as the opening 
message.
Copy that summary → New chat → Paste → Continue with full coherence.


[~1 min]
This is a quick but important one. Every LLM has a context window — think of it as short-term memory. Claude’s is 200K tokens, GPT-4o is 128K, Gemini can go up to a million. Sounds huge, right? But in practice, once you’ve gone back and forth 15 or 20 times, uploaded files, pasted error messages — the model starts to “forget” earlier instructions or subtly contradict itself. Researchers call this the “lost in the middle” problem — LLMs attend most strongly to the beginning and end of their context.
The fix is simple and it works shockingly well. When you feel a conversation getting wobbly — maybe the LLM just forgot a key constraint, or it’s repeating something you already corrected — ask it to summarize the current state.
“Summarize what we’ve built so far. List the key variables, the data sources, what’s working, and what’s still broken. Format it so I can use it as a starting prompt.”
Then you literally open a new chat, paste that summary, and pick up where you left off — but now the model has a clean, focused context instead of 18 messages of conversational drift.
I do this at least once per complex coding session. It takes 30 seconds and saves you from the maddening experience of the LLM “hallucinating” a variable name it made up six messages ago.

CLAUDE.md / AGENT.md
Place in your project root:
# CLAUDE.md
## Project Context
WFRC travel demand model (Cube).
R + sf + data.table. Base pipe.

## Conventions
- EPSG:26912 for all spatial ops
- Snake_case variable names
- Never use `library(tidyverse)`
  — import packages individually

## Data
TAZ shapefile: data/taz_v4.shp
Count stations: data/aadt_2025.csv


[~1.5 min]
Now let’s talk about the next frontier beyond chat-based LLMs: coding agents. These are tools that don’t just suggest code — they can read your entire project, run commands, create files, and iterate on errors autonomously.
The table on the left shows the major players. Claude Code is Anthropic’s terminal-based agent — it’s become very popular, hitting around $2.5 billion in annualized revenue. GitHub Copilot is the one most people know. Cursor is an AI-native code editor. OpenClaw is the open-source wildcard — it started as a weekend project and exploded to nearly 200K GitHub stars. It’s model-agnostic, so you can run it with Claude, GPT, Gemini, or even local models.
Fun fact for the room: just a few days ago — March 31st — Anthropic accidentally shipped Claude Code’s entire source code to the public npm registry. Over 500,000 lines of TypeScript were exposed before they caught it. A packaging error caused by a misconfigured build file. It’s already been forked thousands of times. It’s a good reminder that even the “safety-first” AI lab makes human errors in CI/CD.
Now, the actionable technique on the right: CLAUDE.md files — sometimes called AGENT.md. When you place a markdown file in your project root, coding agents like Claude Code automatically read it as standing instructions. Think of it as a system prompt that lives with your codebase.
For us at WFRC, this is where you encode things like: “always use EPSG:26912,” “use base pipe, not magrittr,” “our TAZ shapefile lives at this path.” Every time the agent spins up, it reads this file and behaves accordingly. It’s like onboarding a new team member, except the team member has perfect memory of the instructions.
If you’re not using coding agents yet, start with Copilot or Claude Code. If you already are, add a CLAUDE.md to your project today.

title: Prompt Engineering Best Practices
text:
6 · Meta-Prompting
Let the LLM write your prompt

I need to write a complex ArcPy script that automates 
network analysis for our regional travel demand model.

Before writing any code:
1. Ask me 3 clarification questions about my data and goals.
2. Then generate the best possible prompt I should use — 
   including role, context, constraints, and output format — 
   so I can paste it back to you (or a different model) 
   for the best result.


Why? The LLM knows what it needs to perform well. Let it tell you.

[~1 min]
This is my favorite technique and it’s the most meta. Instead of struggling to write the perfect prompt yourself, ask the LLM to write the prompt for you.
The example on screen is a real scenario: you need a complex ArcPy script for network analysis. Instead of trying to specify everything upfront — and inevitably forgetting something — you say: “Ask me three clarification questions, then generate the best possible prompt.”
What happens is fascinating. The LLM will ask you things like: “What network dataset are you using — is it an ESRI network dataset or OpenStreetMap?” or “Do you need impedance based on free-flow travel time or congested time?” or “Should the output be a feature class or a CSV of OD travel times?”
These are exactly the details that make the difference between a generic script and one that actually works for your project. The LLM knows what information it needs to produce good output — it just needs permission to ask.
Then it generates a beautifully structured prompt with role, context, constraints, and output format. You can use that prompt in the same chat, or copy it to a different model — maybe you want Claude for the planning and Gemini for the implementation.
This is also great for the official documentation links. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google all publish prompt engineering guides. The core advice converges: be specific, give examples, use structured formatting, and break complex tasks into steps. Meta-prompting automates all of that.

title: Prompt Engineering Best Practices
text:
7 · Before & After Examples


❌ Before (Vague)
Help me with SQL for 
traffic counts.

Make a map of transit 
routes in R.

My pandas script is broken, 
fix it.

✅ After (Engineered)
Act as a SQL Server expert. 
Write a query against our 
traffic_counts table (columns: 
station_id, date, hour, volume, 
direction) that returns AADT by 
station for 2025 using the AASHTO 
factor method. Include comments.
Act as an R/sf developer. 
Using {sf} and base R plotting, 
map UTA TRAX lines from a GTFS 
shapes.txt file. Color lines by 
route_id. Use EPSG:26912.
[Upload the .py file directly]
This script processes the WFRC 
household travel survey. It fails 
at line 47 with a KeyError on 
'trip_mode'. The CSV has columns: 
[list them]. What's wrong?


[~1 min]
Let’s close with concrete before-and-after examples that tie everything together.
The “before” prompts on the left are what most of us start with. They’re not wrong — they’ll get you something. But the “after” prompts on the right incorporate the techniques we’ve covered:
Example one — SQL: We set a role (SQL Server expert), specify the table schema, name the exact calculation method (AASHTO factor), and request comments. That’s role prompting plus schema sharing.
Example two — mapping: We specify the package (sf), the data source (GTFS shapes.txt), the visual encoding (color by route_id), and the CRS. The LLM doesn’t have to guess anything.
Example three — debugging: Instead of saying “it’s broken, fix it,” we upload the actual file, point to the exact line, name the error, and list the columns. This is the difference between a 5-message debugging loop and a one-shot fix.
These patterns come straight from the official guidance. Anthropic’s docs emphasize being explicit and using structured formatting. OpenAI recommends providing context and examples. Google’s best practices say to specify the output format. They all converge on the same core idea: the more precisely you specify the task, the better the result.

title: Modernizing Spatial Workflows
text:
Benchmark 01: Legacy R (sf)
The “Standard” Way: Load everything into RAM, process, output.

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# BENCHMARK 01: Legacy R Stack (sf + CSV/Shapefile)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# FIX (vs previous version):
#
#   force(expr) promise-caching bug:
#     In R, function arguments are lazily evaluated promises whose result is
#     CACHED after the first evaluation. The previous measure_rss() used
#     force(expr) inside a loop, which meant the expression only actually ran
#     on iteration 1 — subsequent iterations timed the cost of returning a
#     cached NULL value (~0 µs). For ITERATIONS > 1 this produced completely
#     wrong median timings.
#
#     Fix: measure_rss() now accepts a function (fn) instead of an expression,
#     and calls fn() on each iteration. Functions are re-invoked every call.
#     Call sites change from measure_rss({ ... }) to measure_rss(function() { ... }).
#
# Author: Pukar Bhandari
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ps)

results_csv <- "_results/benchmark_results.csv"

ITERATIONS <- as.integer(
  Sys.getenv(
    "BENCHMARK_ITERATIONS",
    unset = ifelse(exists("ITERATIONS"), as.character(ITERATIONS), "1")
  )
)

# Helper: accepts a FUNCTION (not a bare expression) and calls it each iteration.
# Using fn() instead of force(expr) ensures the body re-executes every time.
measure_rss <- function(fn, iterations = 1L) {
  times <- numeric(iterations)
  mem_deltas <- numeric(iterations)

  for (i in seq_len(iterations)) {
    gc(verbose = FALSE)
    mem_before <- ps::ps_memory_info()[["rss"]]
    t_start <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]

    fn() # Re-invoked on every iteration — no caching

    t_end <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
    times[i] <- t_end - t_start
    mem_deltas[i] <- (ps::ps_memory_info()[["rss"]] - mem_before) / 1024 / 1024
  }

  list(time_sec = median(times), mem_mb = max(mem_deltas))
}

log_result <- function(sys, lang, op, time_sec, mem_mb) {
  cat(
    sprintf("%s,%s,%s,%.4f,%.2f\n", sys, lang, op, time_sec, mem_mb),
    file = results_csv,
    append = TRUE
  )
}

addr_csv <- "_data/utah_addresses.csv"
county_shp <- "_data/utah_counties.shp"

message("────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────")
message("Running: BENCHMARK 01 - R (sf) Legacy Stack")
message("────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────")

# ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## 2. I/O BENCHMARK (Data Load) ----
# ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

res_io <- measure_rss(
  function() {
    pts <- read_csv(
      addr_csv,
      col_types = cols(CountyID = col_character()),
      show_col_types = FALSE
    ) |>
      filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y)) |> # drop UGRC points with no geometry
      st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 4326)

    cnt <- st_read(county_shp, quiet = TRUE) |>
      st_transform(4326)
  },
  iterations = ITERATIONS
)

log_result("sf", "R", "Load Data", res_io$time_sec, res_io$mem_mb)
message(sprintf(
  "  Load Data: %.3fs | %.1f MB RSS delta",
  res_io$time_sec,
  res_io$mem_mb
))

# ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## 3. RELOAD DATA FOR ANALYSIS PHASE (not timed) ----
# ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

pts <- read_csv(
  addr_csv,
  col_types = cols(CountyID = col_character()),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y)) |> # drop UGRC points with no geometry
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 4326)

cnt <- st_read(county_shp, quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(4326)

# ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## 4. ANALYSIS BENCHMARK (Spatial Join) ----
# ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

res_analysis <- measure_rss(
  function() {
    res_attr <- pts |>
      st_drop_geometry() |>
      count(CountyID)

    res_spatial <- st_join(pts, cnt, join = st_within) |>
      st_drop_geometry() |>
      count(FIPS_ST)
  },
  iterations = ITERATIONS
)

log_result(
  "sf",
  "R",
  "Validation (Join)",
  res_analysis$time_sec,
  res_analysis$mem_mb
)
message(sprintf(
  "  Validation (Join): %.3fs | %.1f MB RSS delta",
  res_analysis$time_sec,
  res_analysis$mem_mb
))

# ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## 5. CLEANUP ----
# ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

rm(pts, cnt, res_attr, res_spatial)

message("────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────")
message("BENCHMARK 01 Complete!")
message("────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────")







Memory Hog


If your dataset is larger than your RAM, this script crashes.
